nodes.title: Linux filesystem and storage (RHCSA): Key Ideas
nodes.content: RHCSA is heavy on filesystem operations: setting permissions with octal notation and special bits, configuring ACLs for fine-grained access, creating LVM logical volumes, mounting filesystems via fstab, and enforcing SELinux contexts. These are tasks performed in the live exam environment, so procedure matters as much as concepts.

flashcards.front: Octal permissions and special bits — what does 4755 mean?
flashcards.back: 4 = setuid bit (run as file owner, not caller), 7 = owner rwx, 5 = group r-x, 5 = other r-x. Special bits: setuid (4) on executables runs as owner; setgid (2) on directories makes new files inherit group; sticky bit (1) on directories prevents non-owners from deleting others' files. `chmod 4755 /usr/bin/passwd` is the classic setuid example.

flashcards.front: ACL vs standard Unix permissions — when do you need an ACL?
flashcards.back: Standard Unix permissions only allow one owner + one group + other. ACLs (set with `setfacl`, viewed with `getfacl`) let you assign specific read/write/execute to individual users or groups beyond those three. Example: you own `/data`, your group is `devs`, but you also want `alice` (not in devs) to have read access — add `setfacl -m u:alice:r /data`. The ACL mask controls the effective maximum.

flashcards.front: LVM — explain PV, VG, LV in one chain.
flashcards.back: Physical Volume (PV): a raw disk or partition initialized for LVM with `pvcreate /dev/sdb`. Volume Group (VG): a pool of PVs combined with `vgcreate vg0 /dev/sdb /dev/sdc` — treated as one large storage pool. Logical Volume (LV): a virtual partition carved from the VG with `lvcreate -L 20G -n data vg0` — formatted and mounted like a normal partition. The LV can be resized online without repartitioning.

flashcards.front: fstab entry — what are the six fields?
flashcards.back: Format: `<device> <mountpoint> <fstype> <options> <dump> <fsck-order>`. Example: `UUID=abc123 /data xfs defaults 0 2`. Field 5 (dump) is almost always 0 (ignore). Field 6 (fsck pass): 1 = root checked first, 2 = checked after root, 0 = skip. Always use UUIDs or LABEL= instead of device names (/dev/sdb) which can shift after reboot.

nodes.title: Security fundamentals: Key Ideas
nodes.content: Security is about layering defenses so no single failure compromises a system. Most exams test the same core ideas: least privilege, defense in depth, the CIA triad, and the shared-responsibility line between you and your cloud provider.

flashcards.front: What is the CIA triad?
flashcards.back: Confidentiality (only the right people see the data), Integrity (data isn't tampered with), Availability (the system is reachable when needed). Every security control maps to at least one of these three pillars.

flashcards.front: What does 'least privilege' mean?
flashcards.back: Grant each identity (user, role, service account) the minimum permissions needed to do its job — no more. The opposite is wildcard access, which makes a single credential leak catastrophic.

flashcards.front: What is defense in depth?
flashcards.back: Stack multiple, independent controls so an attacker has to defeat all of them. Example: WAF in front of an app, network ACL on the subnet, IAM on the workload, encryption at rest in the database.

flashcards.front: Shared responsibility model — who does what?
flashcards.back: The cloud provider secures the cloud (physical hardware, hypervisor, region facilities). You secure what's IN the cloud (your data, IAM config, OS patching on EC2, application code). The exact line shifts by service: serverless is more on the provider, IaaS is more on you.

nodes.title: Networking fundamentals: Key Ideas
nodes.content: Networking moves packets between machines using layered protocols (the OSI / TCP-IP stack). Most exam questions test routing decisions, subnetting math, the difference between L2 and L3, and how DNS / DHCP make the whole thing usable for humans.

flashcards.front: What's the difference between Layer 2 and Layer 3?
flashcards.back: L2 (data link) uses MAC addresses to deliver frames inside a single broadcast domain (a switch). L3 (network) uses IP addresses to route packets between networks (a router). Switches do L2; routers do L3.

flashcards.front: How does a subnet mask work?
flashcards.back: The mask splits an IP into a network portion (the high bits, set to 1) and a host portion (the low bits, set to 0). `/24` means the first 24 bits are network = up to 256 hosts (254 usable). `/30` is 4 IPs = 2 hosts — typical for a point-to-point link.

flashcards.front: What does DNS do?
flashcards.back: Domain Name System translates human-readable names (`example.com`) into IP addresses. A recursive resolver asks the root, the TLD server (`.com`), and finally the authoritative server for the domain. TTL controls how long answers are cached.

flashcards.front: TCP vs UDP — when do you pick each?
flashcards.back: TCP is reliable, ordered, congestion-controlled — use it when every byte matters (HTTP, SSH, SMTP). UDP is lightweight, no handshake, no retransmit — use it for streaming, gaming, DNS queries, anywhere latency beats reliability.

questions.q: Set a STATIC IP `192.168.1.10/24` with gateway `192.168.1.1` and DNS `8.8.8.8` on interface `eth0` using NetworkManager. The change must persist across reboots. Which commands?
choices: `nmcli con mod eth0 ipv4.addresses 192.168.1.10/24 ipv4.gateway 192.168.1.1 ipv4.dns 8.8.8.8 ipv4.method manual && nmcli con up eth0` — persistent NetworkManager configuration

`ip addr add 192.168.1.10/24 dev eth0 && ip route add default via 192.168.1.1` — sets the address and gateway temporarily, but DNS (8.8.8.8) requires a separate `/etc/resolv.conf` edit; lost on reboot
`ifconfig eth0 192.168.1.10 netmask 255.255.255.0 gateway 192.168.1.1` — `ifconfig` is deprecated and `gateway` is not a valid `ifconfig` argument; DNS 8.8.8.8 would still need manual configuration
`vi /etc/network/interfaces` — the Debian/Ubuntu approach to setting IP, gateway, and DNS persistently; RHEL uses NetworkManager with `nmcli` or `nmtui`, not `/etc/network/interfaces`
questions.explanation: nmcli con mod CONNECTION ipv4.addresses IP/MASK ipv4.gateway GW ipv4.dns DNS ipv4.method manual. Then nmcli con up CONNECTION. Persistent. nmcli con show: list connections. nmcli device status: device states. Alternatively: edit /etc/NetworkManager/system-connections/CONNECTION.nmconnection.

questions.q: Linux name-to-IP resolution consults a CONFIGURABLE list of sources (by default `files` then `dns`, defined in `/etc/nsswitch.conf`). The `files` source reads from `/etc/hosts`. An entry in `/etc/hosts` like `10.0.5.42 internal.example.com` overrides DNS for that name. What is `/etc/hosts`?
choices: Replaces /etc/resolv.conf — false; resolv.conf configures DNS servers, hosts maps names locally
Localhost-only — false; can store any local override
Hostname-only — false; that's `/etc/hostname`
Local hostname → IP override map
questions.explanation: /etc/hosts: IP FQDN aliases per line. /etc/nsswitch.conf hosts: files dns — 'files' means check /etc/hosts first. For testing: add temporary entry. /etc/resolv.conf: DNS server configuration (nameserver IP, domain, search). hostnamectl: set system hostname. dnsdomainname: show domain. checked before DNS per /etc/nsswitch.conf

questions.q: A router shows `10.2.0.0/24 via 192.168.1.254` is not reachable. The admin needs to add a route for that network. They want both: TEMPORARY (current session, lost on reboot) and PERSISTENT (survives reboot). Which approach?
choices: `netstat route add` — `netstat` doesn't add routes; netstat cannot add a temporary or persistent route to the routing table
`route add NETWORK/MASK GW` — `route` is deprecated on modern RHEL; doesn't persist
Temporary: `ip route add 10.2.0.0/24 via 192.168.1.254`
`ifconfig route add` — ifconfig doesn't manage routes
questions.explanation: Temporary: ip route add 192.168.10.0/24 via 10.0.0.1 (lost on reboot). Permanent (NetworkManager): nmcli con mod CONNECTION ipv4.routes '192.168.10.0/24 10.0.0.1' then nmcli con up CONNECTION. Or edit connection file. ip route show: display routing table. Permanent: nmcli con mod CON ipv4.routes

questions.q: An admin needs to see (a) every TCP/UDP socket in LISTEN state, (b) the local + remote address + port, (c) the process / pid / executable that owns each socket. Which command provides all of this in ONE invocation?
choices: `netstat -r` — routing table only, no sockets/processes
`ss -tulnp`
`ip link show` — interface state, no sockets
`ifconfig -a` — interface config, no sockets
questions.explanation: ss -tulnp: -t TCP, -u UDP, -l listening, -n numeric (no name resolution), -p show process. Shows: port, state, PID, process name. Requires root for all PIDs. netstat -tulnp: older equivalent (net-tools package). lsof -i :80: what's using port 80. firewall-cmd --list-ports: what's open in firewall.

questions.q: A RHEL host needs to mount an NFS share `nfsserver:/share` at `/mnt/nfs`. The mount must be PERSISTENT (survives reboot). Which sequence?
choices: `mount -t nfs nfsserver:/share /mnt/nfs`
`mount --type=nfs nfsserver/share /mnt` — wrong syntax (missing colon)
`smbmount` — SMB, not NFS
`nfsmount` — not a real command
questions.explanation: Temporary: mount -t nfs nfsserver:/share /mnt/nfs. Persistent /etc/fstab: nfsserver:/share /mnt/nfs nfs defaults,_netdev 0 0. _netdev: wait for network before mounting. nfsstat: show NFS stats. showmount -e nfsserver: list server exports. Install nfs-utils first: dnf install nfs-utils. add to /etc/fstab for persistence

questions.q: An admin bonds two physical NICs `eth0` + `eth1` into a single `bond0` interface for active-backup redundancy. Configuration must persist via NetworkManager. Which `nmcli` sequence?
choices: `bonding --create` — not a real command; bonding --create is not a real command and cannot configure an active-backup bond interface
`nmcli con add type bond ifname bond0 mode active-backup`
`nmcli bond create` — wrong syntax
`ip link add bond0 type bond` — works at runtime but doesn't persist via NetworkManager
questions.explanation: Create bond: nmcli con add type bond ifname bond0 bond.options 'mode=active-backup'. Add slaves: nmcli con add type ethernet ifname eth0 master bond0; nmcli con add type ethernet ifname eth1 master bond0. Activate: nmcli con up bond0. cat /proc/net/bonding/bond0: check status. Modes: active-backup, balance-rr, 802.3ad (LACP). add slaves with nmcli ethernet con

nodes.title: Linux user and group management: Key Ideas
nodes.content: RHCSA exams heavily test creating, modifying, and deleting users and groups, managing passwords, and setting file permissions using standard Linux commands and /etc/passwd, /etc/shadow, /etc/group.

flashcards.front: Command to create a user with a specific UID and home directory?
flashcards.back: useradd -u 1050 -m -d /home/alice alice  (-m creates the home, -d sets the path, -u sets UID).

flashcards.front: Difference between usermod -aG and usermod -G?
flashcards.back: -aG appends the user to a group (keeping existing memberships). -G alone replaces all supplementary groups — omitting -a removes the user from any groups not listed.

flashcards.front: How to lock and unlock a user account?
flashcards.back: passwd -l <user> locks (prepends ! to the password hash). passwd -u <user> unlocks. usermod -L / -U does the same.

flashcards.front: /etc/passwd format?
flashcards.back: username:x:UID:GID:comment:home:shell — 'x' means the password hash is in /etc/shadow. A UID of 0 means root privileges.

questions.q: Create a new user `bob` with UID 1500, default shell `/bin/bash`, and a home directory `/home/bob`. The home directory should be created automatically with the user. Which `useradd` invocation is correct?
choices: `useradd bob --uid 1500 --home /home/bob` — creates the user but `--uid` and `--home` are not valid short flags; correct flags are `-u` and `-d`; also omits `-s` for shell; this is not a canonical invocation because --uid and --home are not valid useradd flags
`useradd -u 1500 -m -s /bin/bash bob` — specifies UID 1500 (`-u`), creates the home directory (`-m`), sets the default shell (`-s`), and then the username; canonical invocation
`adduser -uid 1500 -shell /bin/bash bob` — `adduser` is a higher-level interactive wrapper; `-uid` is not a valid flag; use `useradd` for scriptable user creation with explicit UID
`usermod -u 1500 -s /bin/bash bob` — `usermod` modifies an existing user record; `bob` must already exist; `useradd` creates the user and home directory from scratch
questions.explanation: useradd -u 1500 -m -s /bin/bash bob: -u UID, -m create home, -s shell. Set password: passwd bob. -g primary group: -g groupname. -G supplementary groups: -G wheel,docker. View: id bob. Modify existing user: usermod. Delete: userdel -r bob (remove home).

questions.q: An admin needs to add user `alice` to the existing supplementary group `wheel` (so she gains sudo privileges) WITHOUT removing her from any other groups. Which command preserves existing group memberships and adds wheel?
choices: `groupadd wheel alice` — `groupadd` creates groups, doesn't add users
`addgroup alice wheel` — Debian/Ubuntu syntax, not RHEL
`usermod -aG wheel alice`
`gpasswd -a wheel alice` — argument order reversed; correct order is `gpasswd -a alice wheel`
questions.explanation: usermod -aG wheel username: -a (append, don't replace other groups), -G (supplementary group). Without -a: replaces ALL supplementary groups! gpasswd -a username wheel: alternative. id username: verify. User needs to re-login for group change to take effect (or: newgrp wheel in current session).

questions.q: An admin needs to enforce a PASSWORD-AGING policy on user `alice`: max age 90 days, warn 7 days before expiry. The command modifies `/etc/shadow` aging fields. Which?
choices: `passwd --expire alice` — IMMEDIATELY expires, doesn't set max age policy
`chage -M 90 -W 7 alice`
`usermod --password-age` — `usermod` doesn't have password-aging flags; that's chage's job
`passwdage --set` — not a real command
questions.explanation: chage -M 90: max days before password must change. -m 1: minimum days between changes. -W 7: warn 7 days before expiry. -l username: list current aging info. -E 2025-12-31: account expiry date. -I 30: days after expiry before account locked. /etc/login.defs: PASS_MAX_DAYS for system default.

questions.q: Linux stores user accounts in TWO files: (A) world-readable, listing UID + GID + GECOS + home + shell — NO password. (B) ROOT-readable only, holding hashed password + aging fields. The split protects password hashes from world readers while keeping basic user info available. Which mapping?
choices: `/etc/passwd` (world-readable
Identical files — false; the files are not identical — /etc/passwd is world-readable while /etc/shadow is root-readable only
/etc/shadow deprecated — false; still used
Both store plaintext — false; passwd has 'x' placeholder, shadow has hash
questions.explanation: /etc/passwd format: username:x:UID:GID:comment:home:shell. /etc/shadow: username:HASH:lastchange:min:max:warn:inactive:expire. HASH format: $6$ = SHA-512. chage: modify shadow aging. pwck: check passwd consistency. unshadow: combine for cracking (John the Ripper). /etc/shadow stores hashed passwords (root-only)

nodes.title: Mixed exam topics: Key Ideas
nodes.content: Some exam objectives don't fit neatly into a single domain — they span protocols, tools, or concepts covered briefly in multiple sections. These cards treat each item as a stand-alone fact, the way an exam question presents it: one concept, one answer.

flashcards.front: What is the difference between a hub, a switch, and a router?
flashcards.back: Hub: Layer 1, repeats every frame to all ports — all devices share bandwidth, collisions guaranteed. Switch: Layer 2, forwards frames using a MAC address table to only the destination port — full duplex, no collisions, each port gets full bandwidth. Router: Layer 3, makes forwarding decisions based on IP address, connects different networks. Hub is legacy; switches dominate LAN; routers are at network edges.

flashcards.front: What is RAID 5 and how many drives can it tolerate losing?
flashcards.back: RAID 5 stripes data and parity across at least 3 drives. Any single drive failure can be recovered by reconstructing missing data from the remaining drives and parity. It cannot tolerate 2 simultaneous drive failures. Effective capacity = (N-1) × drive size. Read performance is excellent; write requires parity recalculation. RAID 6 tolerates 2 failures using double parity.

flashcards.front: What does a proxy server do, and how does a forward proxy differ from a reverse proxy?
flashcards.back: Forward proxy: sits between clients and the internet on behalf of clients — used for content filtering, caching, and anonymizing outbound requests (the server sees the proxy's IP). Reverse proxy: sits in front of servers on behalf of the server — used for load balancing, SSL termination, caching, and hiding backend topology (the client sees the proxy's IP). Both intermediate HTTP, but they protect opposite sides.

flashcards.front: What is the purpose of a DMZ in network architecture?
flashcards.back: A demilitarized zone is a network segment between the untrusted internet and the trusted internal network, typically protected by two firewalls (or two interfaces on one firewall). Public-facing services (web, email, DNS) sit in the DMZ: internet can reach them but not the internal network; if the DMZ host is compromised, the inner firewall still blocks access to the internal LAN.
